steps.title: Counting eggs by the crate
steps.display: 1 crate = 30 eggs  |  1 mole = 6.02 × 10^{23} particles
working: Market seller counts crates, not single eggs.
Chemist counts moles, not single atoms or molecules.
steps.narration: At a Nigerian market, sellers pack eggs into crates instead of counting them one by one. Chemists pack tiny particles into moles the same way.

steps.title: Moles from mass, s.t.p. volume, and particles
steps.narration: So how do you get moles? It depends on what the question gives you. Grams? Divide by the molar mass. A gas volume at s.t.p.? Divide by twenty two point four. A number of particles? Divide by six point zero two times ten to the twenty three. Three doors into the same room. Whichever door you use, you end up in moles.

steps.title: Percentage composition by mass
steps.display: % element = \frac{mass of element in 1 mol}{molar mass of compound} × 100%
working: Calcium trioxonitrate(V) (calcium nitrate), Ca(NO_{3})_{2}:
steps.narration: Percentage composition asks one thing. Out of the whole compound, how much is this one element? First add up every atom to get the molar mass. Be careful with brackets, because the small number outside multiplies everything inside. Then take the mass of your element, divide by the total, and times one hundred. It works like your share of a shared plate of jollof.

steps.title: Empirical and molecular formula
steps.display: MF = (EF)_{n}  |  n = \frac{M}{m_{EF}}  |  M = 2 × vapour density
steps.narration: The empirical formula is the simplest ratio of atoms, like a recipe for one small pot. The molecular formula is the real molecule, the big pot. To get the small recipe, change each mass to moles, then divide by the smallest. To get the big pot, see how many small recipes fit into the real molar mass. If you get vapour density, double it first.

steps.title: Balancing equations and conservation of mass
steps.display: Adjust coefficients only (never subscripts)  |  (s), (l), (g), (aq)
working: Unbalanced: H_{2}(g) + O_{2}(g) → H_{2}O(l)
4 H atoms and 2 O atoms on each side (mass conserved)
steps.narration: Atoms are never created or destroyed in a reaction. They just change partners. So both sides must have the same number of each atom. To balance, you may only change the big numbers in front. Never touch the small numbers inside a formula. Changing those turns water into a different substance entirely.

steps.title: Reacting masses and gas volumes
steps.display: n_{unknown} = n_{known} × \frac{coeff_{unknown}}{coeff_{known}}
steps.narration: Here is the golden habit. Never compare grams across a reaction, because different substances weigh differently. Change what you know into moles first. Then use the balanced equation like an exchange rate. One mole of this gives two moles of that, for example. Finally, change your answer back into grams or volume.

steps.title: Limiting reagent and excess reactant
steps.display: Compare \frac{n_{available}}{coeff} → smallest value is the limiting reagent
working: Mix 3 mol H_{2} with 2 mol O_{2}:
H_{2} limits product (3 mol H_{2}O formed; 0.5 mol O_{2} left)
steps.narration: Think of making sandwiches. You need two slices of bread for each piece of meat. If the bread runs out first, you stop, even with meat left over. The bread is the limiting reagent. In chemistry, divide what you have by the number in the equation. The smaller result runs out first, and it decides how much product you get.

steps.title: Read the reaction and convert given mass to moles
steps.display: 4.8 g Mg + 0.30 mol HCl: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl_{2}(aq) + H_{2}(g). Find V_{s.t.p.}(H_{2}).
working: M(Mg) = 24 g mol^{−1}
n(HCl) = 0.30 mol (given)
steps.narration: Let's try one together. Before anything else, change everything into moles. Magnesium weighs twenty four grams per mole, so four point eight grams gives zero point two zero moles. The acid is already in moles, zero point three zero. Now we can compare them fairly.

steps.title: Identify the limiting reagent
steps.display: 1 mol Mg requires 2 mol HCl
working: 0.20 mol Mg needs 2 × 0.20 = 0.40 mol HCl
Available HCl = 0.30 mol < 0.40 mol
HCl is the limiting reagent (Mg is in excess)
steps.narration: Now the big question. Which one runs out first? The equation says each magnesium needs two acids. So zero point two zero moles of magnesium would need zero point four zero moles of acid. We only have zero point three zero. Not enough! So the acid runs out first. Magnesium is left over.

steps.title: Use the limiting reagent to find moles and volume of hydrogen
steps.narration: Since the acid runs out first, the acid decides how much hydrogen we get. Two acids give one hydrogen, so take half. Half of zero point three zero is zero point one five moles. Each mole of gas at s.t.p. takes up twenty two point four cubic decimetres. Multiply, and you get three point three six. That is our answer.

steps.title: Restate the JAMB past question
steps.display: A compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. Its relative molecular mass is 180. Find its molecular formula. (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
working: Assume 100 g sample → 40.0 g C, 6.7 g H, 53.3 g O
Target: molecular formula (M_{r} = 180)
steps.narration: Now a real JAMB question, from twenty twelve. We are given percentages, not grams. Here is a nice trick. Pretend you have exactly one hundred grams. Then forty percent carbon simply becomes forty grams of carbon. The percentages turn straight into grams, and the hard part is gone.

steps.title: Divide masses by relative atomic masses
steps.display: n_{element} = \frac{mass}{A_{r}}
steps.narration: Why can't we just compare the grams? Because a carbon atom is much heavier than a hydrogen atom. Grams don't tell us how many atoms. Moles do. So divide each mass by its atomic mass. Carbon gives about three point three three. Hydrogen gives six point seven. Oxygen gives three point three three again. See how carbon and oxygen match? Keep that in mind.

steps.title: Divide by the smallest mole value to get the empirical formula
steps.display: Smallest mole amount = 3.33  →  Empirical formula = CH_{2}O
steps.narration: We want small whole numbers, so divide everything by the smallest value, three point three three. Carbon becomes one. Hydrogen becomes about two. Oxygen becomes one. So the simplest recipe is one carbon, two hydrogens, one oxygen. That is C H two O.

steps.title: Scale the empirical formula to the relative molecular mass
working: Molecular formula = (CH_{2}O)_{6} = C_{6}H_{12}O_{6}
steps.narration: Careful, many students stop here and lose the mark! The question wants the real molecule. One C H two O weighs only thirty. The real molecule weighs one hundred and eighty. How many thirties fit into one hundred and eighty? Six. So multiply every atom by six. You get C six H twelve O six, which is glucose.

steps.title: Diatomic molecules and bracket subscripts
working: H_{2}, N_{2}, O_{2}, F_{2}, Cl_{2}, Br_{2}, I_{2} are diatomic gases.
Ca(NO_{3})_{2} has 1 Ca, 2 N, and 6 O atoms (M = 164).
steps.narration: This trap catches many students. Oxygen gas is not single atoms. It travels in pairs, so one mole of oxygen gas weighs thirty two, not sixteen. Hydrogen, nitrogen, chlorine and the other halogens pair up the same way. And when you see a bracket, the number outside multiplies everything inside. Two nitrate groups means two nitrogens.

steps.title: Empirical formula versus molecular formula and vapour density
steps.display: Wrong: stopping at EF or using M = VD  |  Right: M = 2 × VD, then MF = (EF)_{n}
steps.narration: Two quick traps here. First, read what the question wants. Empirical or molecular? JAMB often puts the wrong one among the options. Second, vapour density is not the molar mass. It is only half of it. So if vapour density is forty five, the molar mass is ninety.

steps.title: Equation ratios and excess left over
steps.display: Wrong: 1000 cm^{3} H_{2} + 300 cm^{3} O_{2} → 700 cm^{3} left  |  Right: 600 cm^{3} used, 400 cm^{3} left
steps.narration: Gases do not react one to one just because you poured them together. Look at the equation. Two hydrogens go with every one oxygen. So three hundred of oxygen uses up six hundred of hydrogen, not three hundred. We started with one thousand of hydrogen, so four hundred is left over.

steps.title: Moles are the bridge for every chemical calculation
steps.display: Given (mass, volume, particles) → Moles → Balanced mole ratio → Target
working: Check subscripts, balance the equation, find the limiting reagent, then solve.
steps.narration: Here is the whole lesson in one idea. Moles are the bridge. Whatever the question gives you, cross into moles first. Use the balanced equation to move from one substance to another. Then cross back to grams or volume. Do this every time, and mole questions stop being scary.

quickCheck.stem: Which sample contains the same number of constituent molecules as the number of atoms in 24 g of magnesium? Use Mg = 24, H = 1, O = 16 and Cl = 35.5.

options.why: M(H_{2}) = 2 g mol^{−1}, so 1 g of H_{2} is only 0.5 mol of molecules, half of 1 mol.
Oxygen gas is diatomic with M(O_{2}) = 32 g mol^{−1}, so 16 g is only 0.5 mol of molecules.
24 g of Mg is \frac{24}{24} = 1 mol of atoms, and 32 g of O_{2} is \frac{32}{32} = 1 mol of molecules, so both contain N_{A} particles.
Chlorine gas is diatomic with M(Cl_{2}) = 71 g mol^{−1}, so 35.5 g is only 0.5 mol of molecules.

steps.title: Hot sun on a car tyre
steps.display: Heat up trapped air → faster molecules → more wall hits → higher pressure
working: Pump air into a tyre, press harder to shrink it, or warm it in afternoon sun.
steps.narration: Leave a tyre in hot sun. The air inside warms up. Its tiny particles speed up and hit the walls harder. That harder push is higher pressure.

steps.title: Kelvin conversion and standard conditions (s.t.p.)
working: Absolute zero = 0 K (−273 °C)
1 mol ideal gas at s.t.p. = 22.4 dm^{3} (1 dm^{3} = 1000 cm^{3})
steps.narration: Before any gas law, change Celsius to kelvin. Why? Because kelvin starts at true zero, where particles stop moving. Celsius zero is just where water freezes. So add two hundred and seventy three. Twenty seven degrees becomes three hundred kelvin. Also remember s.t.p. It means zero degrees Celsius and seven hundred and sixty millimetres of mercury.

steps.title: Boyle's law, Charles's law, and the pressure law
steps.display: Boyle (const T): P_{1}V_{1} = P_{2}V_{2}  |  Charles (const P): \frac{V_{1}}{T_{1}} = \frac{V_{2}}{T_{2}}  |  Pressure (const V): \frac{P_{1}}{T_{1}} = \frac{P_{2}}{T_{2}}
working: Boyle: P doubled → V halved (P_{1} = 2 atm, V_{1} = 6 dm^{3} → P_{2} = 3 atm, V_{2} = 4 dm^{3})
Pressure law: P_{1} = 1.0 atm at 300 K → at 600 K, P_{2} = 2.0 atm
steps.narration: Three simple laws, each keeping one thing fixed. Squeeze a gas at the same temperature, and its volume shrinks. Double the pressure, half the volume. That is Boyle. Heat it at the same pressure, and it expands. That is Charles. Heat it in a closed tin, and the pressure rises. That is the pressure law. Twice the kelvin, twice the pressure.

steps.title: General gas equation and ideal gas equation
working: Combined law handles changing P, V, and T for fixed n.
PV = nRT uses R = 0.082 atm dm^{3} K^{−1} mol^{−1} (P in atm, V in dm^{3})
steps.narration: What if pressure, volume and temperature all change together? Then join the three laws into one. P V over T before equals P V over T after. And when a question talks about moles, use P V equals n R T. Just make sure your units match the R you choose. With atmospheres and cubic decimetres, R is zero point zero eight two.

steps.title: Dalton's law of partial pressures
steps.display: P_{total} = P_{1} + P_{2} + ...  |  P_{i} = \frac{n_{i}}{n_{total}} P_{total}  |  P_{dry} = P_{total} − P_{water}
working: Mixture: 1 mol A + 3 mol B at P_{total} = 2.0 atm → P_{A} = \frac{1}{4} × 2.0 = 0.50 atm
Over water at 760 mmHg if P_{water} = 20 mmHg → P_{dry} = 760 − 20 = 740 mmHg
steps.narration: In a mixture, each gas pushes on the walls by itself. Add all the pushes, and you get the total pressure. A gas gets a share that matches its share of the moles. One mole out of four gets a quarter of the pressure. And gas collected over water is wet. Take away the water vapour pressure to get the dry gas.

steps.title: Gay-Lussac's law and Avogadro's law
steps.display: Gay-Lussac: reacting gas volumes bear simple whole-number ratios  |  Avogadro: V ∝ n (const T, P)
working: 2CO(g) + O_{2}(g) → 2CO_{2}(g)  (2 vol : 1 vol : 2 vol)
Equal gas volumes at the same T and P hold equal numbers of molecules.
steps.narration: Gases react in simple volume ratios, like two to one. Why? Avogadro explains it. Equal volumes of gases, at the same temperature and pressure, hold the same number of molecules. So volumes behave just like moles. If the equation says two to one, then forty cubic centimetres reacts with twenty.

steps.title: Graham's law of diffusion
working: Compare H_{2} (M = 2) and O_{2} (M = 32):
\frac{r(H_{2})}{r(O_{2})} = \sqrt{\frac{32}{2}} = \sqrt{16} = 4  →  H_{2} diffuses 4 times faster
steps.narration: Light gases move faster than heavy ones. Think of a small boy and a big man racing through a crowd. But it is not a simple ratio. You take the square root of the masses. Hydrogen is sixteen times lighter than oxygen. The square root of sixteen is four, so hydrogen moves four times faster.

steps.title: List variables and convert Celsius to kelvin
steps.display: A gas occupies 300 cm^{3} at 27 °C and 760 mmHg. Find its volume at 127 °C and 380 mmHg.
steps.narration: Let's try one. First, write down what you know, before and after. Volume three hundred, pressure seven hundred and sixty. Now the temperatures. Never use Celsius here! Twenty seven plus two hundred and seventy three is three hundred kelvin. One hundred and twenty seven becomes four hundred kelvin.

steps.title: Rearrange the general gas equation for the final volume
working: Check units: P_{1} and P_{2} are both mmHg; V_{1} is cm^{3}, so V_{2} is cm^{3}.
steps.narration: Which law do we use? Pressure changes, temperature changes, and volume changes too. All three are moving, so we need the combined equation. We want the new volume, so we make it the subject. Both pressures are in the same unit, so they cancel nicely. No conversion needed.

steps.title: Substitute values and check physical sense
steps.narration: Now put the numbers in. Three hundred over three hundred is one. Seven hundred and sixty over three hundred and eighty is two. So the answer is two times four hundred, which is eight hundred. Does that make sense? Yes. We lowered the pressure and raised the temperature. Both make a gas expand.

steps.title: Restate the JAMB past question
steps.display: A volume of 200 cm^{3} of oxygen diffuses through a porous plug in 50 s. How long will 80 cm^{3} of methane, CH_{4}, take under the same conditions? (O = 16, C = 12, H = 1)
steps.narration: Now a real JAMB question, from twenty sixteen. Oxygen and methane are racing through the same tiny holes. But they have different volumes to push through. So we can't just compare times. We first find oxygen's speed, then use it to find methane's.

steps.title: Find oxygen's diffusion rate and the Graham's law ratio
steps.narration: Oxygen moves two hundred in fifty seconds. That is four cubic centimetres every second. Now, who is faster? Methane weighs sixteen and oxygen weighs thirty two. Methane is lighter, so it is faster. Thirty two over sixteen is two. Take the square root. Methane is root two times faster than oxygen.

steps.title: Divide methane's volume by methane's rate to find time
steps.narration: Time equals volume divided by speed. Methane needs to move eighty. Its speed is four root two. Eighty over four is twenty. Twenty over root two is about fourteen. So methane takes about fourteen seconds. That fits, because it has less gas to move and moves faster.

steps.title: Never plug degrees Celsius into a gas law
steps.display: Wrong: T = 20 °C in PV = nRT or Charles's law  |  Right: T = 20 + 273 = 293 K
working: Doubling both P and V quadruples T in Kelvin (273 K → 1092 K).
At 20 °C, n = \frac{8.2 × 2.93}{0.082 × 293} = 1.00 mol (using 20 gives a huge error).
steps.narration: This is the number one gas law mistake. Never put Celsius into a gas law. Twenty degrees Celsius is not twenty. It is two hundred and ninety three kelvin. If you use twenty, your answer will be wildly wrong. Add two hundred and seventy three every single time, even when you are in a hurry.

steps.title: Subtract water vapour pressure and check which gas is asked
steps.display: Wrong: P_{dry} = 765 mmHg (wet) or picking P(N_{2}) for P(O_{2})  |  Right: P_{dry} = 765 − 5 = 760 mmHg
working: Gas over water: P_{dry} = P_{total} − P_{water vapour}.
steps.narration: Two more traps. Gas collected over water carries water vapour with it. So take away the vapour pressure before you do anything else. Seven hundred and sixty five take away five leaves seven hundred and sixty. And in a mixture, read the question again. Make sure you give the pressure of the gas it asked for.

steps.title: Remember the square root in Graham's law
steps.display: Wrong: \frac{r_{X}}{r_{Y}} = \frac{M_{Y}}{M_{X}} → 2 × 28 = 56  |  Right: \left(\frac{r_{X}}{r_{Y}}\right)^{2} = \frac{M_{Y}}{M_{X}} → 4 × 28 = 112
working: If X (M = 28) diffuses twice as fast as Y, 2 = \sqrt{\frac{M_{Y}}{28}}.
Square both sides: 4 = \frac{M_{Y}}{28} → M_{Y} = 112.
steps.narration: Students often forget the square root here. If a gas moves twice as fast, its partner is not twice as heavy. Square the two first. Two squared is four, so the other gas is four times as heavy. Four times twenty eight gives one hundred and twelve.

steps.title: Kelvin first, dry pressure second, right law third
steps.display: T → Kelvin  |  Gas over water → P_{total} − P_{water}  |  Match P, V, T, n, or \sqrt{M}
working: Convert to kelvin, strip out water vapour if wet, and pick the matching gas law.
steps.narration: So for every gas question, carry three habits. First, change Celsius to kelvin. Second, if the gas is wet, take away the water vapour. Third, ask what is changing, then choose the law that fits. Get those three right, and most gas questions become easy marks.

quickCheck.stem: A 50 cm^{3} gas sample is collected over water at 10 °C and 765 mmHg. Water vapour pressure is 5 mmHg. What volume would the dry gas occupy at 0 °C and 760 mmHg?

options.why: 49.19 cm^{3} uses too small a kelvin temperature ratio.
48.87 cm^{3} does not match the 273 K to 283 K cooling ratio.
48.55 cm^{3} uses the wet total pressure of 765 mmHg instead of subtracting 5 mmHg.

steps.title: Lime juice meets wood ash water
steps.display: Sour lime (acid) + wood-ash water (alkali) → milder salt + water
working: Sharp sourness vs slippery bitterness
Mix the right amounts → they cancel out
steps.narration: Fresh lime tastes sharply sour while wood ash water feels soapy. Mix the exact right amounts together and they cancel out into milder salt and water.

steps.title: Strong vs weak and basicity
steps.display: Strong: complete ionisation (→)   |   Weak: partial ionisation (⇌)
working: HCl + H_{2}O → H_{3}O^{+} + Cl^{-}  (strong, high conductivity)
CH_{3}COOH + H_{2}O ⇌ H_{3}O^{+} + CH_{3}COO^{-}  (weak, basicity = 1)
H_{2}SO_{4} → 2H^{+} + SO_{4}^{2-}  (dibasic, basicity = 2)
steps.narration: Strong and weak is not about how dangerous an acid feels. It is about breaking apart in water. A strong acid like hydrochloric acid breaks up completely. A weak acid like vinegar breaks up only a little. Basicity is different again. It counts how many hydrogen ions one acid can give. Sulphuric acid gives two, so it is dibasic.

steps.title: The pH and pOH scales
working: 10^{-3} mol/dm^{3} HCl → pH = 3;   10^{-3} mol/dm^{3} NaOH → pOH = 3, pH = 11
steps.narration: The p H scale tells you how acidic something is, from zero to fourteen. Below seven is acidic. Seven is neutral. Above seven is alkaline. There is a shortcut for powers of ten. If the acid has ten to the minus three of hydrogen ions, the p H is three. And p H plus p O H always makes fourteen.

steps.title: Neutralisation and indicators
working: Strong acid + strong base → any indicator (pH jump 4 to 10)
Strong acid + weak base (e.g. Na_{2}CO_{3}) → methyl orange (red acid, yellow alkali)
Weak acid + strong base → phenolphthalein (colourless acid, pink alkali)
steps.narration: When an acid meets an alkali, hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions join to make water. That is neutralisation. An indicator tells you when it happens by changing colour. Choose it based on which side is weak. Weak alkali? Use methyl orange. Weak acid? Use phenolphthalein. Both strong? Either one works.

steps.title: Concentration and titration ratio
steps.display: \frac{C_{A} V_{A}}{C_{B} V_{B}} = \frac{n_{A}}{n_{B}}     and     Conc (g/dm^{3}) = Conc (mol/dm^{3}) × Molar mass
working: Dilution: C_{1} V_{1} = C_{2} V_{2}  (moles stay constant)
steps.narration: Concentration is how much is dissolved in each cubic decimetre. Always change cubic centimetres to cubic decimetres, by dividing by one thousand. For titration, the balanced equation gives the ratio. One sulphuric acid reacts with two sodium hydroxides. Put that ratio in the formula, and the rest is substitution.

steps.title: Types of salts and hydrolysis
steps.display: Salts: normal (NaCl), acid (NaHSO_{4}), basic (Zn(OH)Cl), double (KAl(SO_{4})_{2}·12H_{2}O)
working: Strong acid + strong base (NaCl) → neutral (pH = 7)
Strong acid + weak base (NH_{4}Cl) → acidic (NH_{4}^{+} + H_{2}O ⇌ NH_{3} + H_{3}O^{+})
Weak acid + strong base (Na_{2}CO_{3}) → alkaline (CO_{3}^{2-} + H_{2}O ⇌ HCO_{3}^{-} + OH^{-})
Insoluble salts (AgCl, BaSO_{4}) → prepared by double decomposition
steps.narration: Not every salt is neutral. It depends on its parents. A strong acid with a strong base gives a neutral salt, like table salt. A strong acid with a weak base gives an acidic salt, like ammonium chloride. A weak acid with a strong base gives an alkaline salt, like washing soda. The stronger parent wins.

steps.title: Read the mass, volume, and goal
steps.display: Find the pH at 25 °C of 0.80 g NaOH in 200 cm^{3} solution. (Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)
working: Goal: find pH via concentration and pOH
steps.narration: Let's try one. We want the p H of some sodium hydroxide. But we can't jump straight to p H. We need the concentration in moles per cubic decimetre first. So the plan is grams, then moles per cubic decimetre, then p O H, then p H.

steps.title: Find g/dm^{3} and mol/dm^{3}
working: Molar mass of NaOH = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40 g/mol
Molar conc = \frac{4.0}{40} = 0.10 mol/dm^{3} = 10^{-1} mol/dm^{3}
steps.narration: Two hundred cubic centimetres is zero point two cubic decimetres. So zero point eight grams in zero point two gives four grams per cubic decimetre. Now change grams to moles. Sodium hydroxide weighs forty. Four over forty is zero point one. That is ten to the minus one.

steps.title: Use strong-base dissociation
steps.narration: Sodium hydroxide is a strong alkali, so it breaks up completely. Every unit gives one hydroxide ion. So the hydroxide is also ten to the minus one. Using our shortcut, the power is minus one, so the p O H is one. Careful, that is not the answer yet.

steps.title: Convert pOH to pH
working: Check: pH 13 > 7, strongly alkaline as expected for NaOH
steps.narration: We want p H, not p O H. Remember they add up to fourteen. So fourteen minus one gives thirteen. Does it make sense? Yes. Sodium hydroxide is a strong alkali, so we expect a high number, well above seven.

steps.title: Read the titration question
steps.display: A 15.00 cm^{3} sample of H_{2}SO_{4} neutralizes 25.00 cm^{3} of 0.125 mol/dm^{3} NaOH. Find [H_{2}SO_{4}].
steps.narration: Now a real JAMB titration question. We know the sodium hydroxide fully, both its volume and its concentration. For the acid, we only know the volume. So the acid concentration is what we need to find.

steps.title: Balance the equation first
working: n_{A} = 1 mol H_{2}SO_{4},   n_{B} = 2 mol NaOH
Acid-to-base mole ratio = 1 : 2
steps.narration: Before any numbers, write the balanced equation. This step decides the answer! One sulphuric acid needs two sodium hydroxides, because it has two hydrogens to give away. So the ratio of acid to base is one to two, not one to one.

steps.title: Apply the titration formula
working: Volumes V_{A} and V_{B} are both in cm^{3}, so units cancel
steps.narration: Now fill in the formula with that one to two ratio. Both volumes are in cubic centimetres. Since they are the same unit, they cancel out. So there is no need to change them to cubic decimetres here.

steps.title: Calculate the acid concentration
steps.narration: Rearrange and calculate. Zero point one two five times twenty five gives three point one two five. Two times fifteen gives thirty. Three point one two five over thirty is about zero point one zero four. You can check it with moles too, and you get the same answer.

steps.title: Do not assume a 1 : 1 ratio or count all H atoms
steps.display: Wrong: \frac{C_{A} V_{A}}{C_{B} V_{B}} = \frac{1}{1} for H_{2}SO_{4}   |   Right: \frac{n_{A}}{n_{B}} = \frac{1}{2}
working: H_{2}SO_{4} is dibasic (n_{A} = 1 reacts with 2 NaOH)
CH_{3}COOH has 4 H atoms, but only 1 ionisable H^{+} (basicity = 1)
steps.narration: The biggest titration trap is assuming one to one. Sulphuric acid has two hydrogens to give, so it needs twice as much alkali. Another trap is ethanoic acid. It has four hydrogens, but only one of them can leave as an ion. So its basicity is one, not four.

steps.title: Do not report pOH as the pH of an alkali
steps.display: 0.001 mol/dm^{3} NaOH:   Wrong: pH = 3   |   Right: pOH = 3 → pH = 14 - 3 = 11
working: NaOH and KOH furnish OH^{-}, not H_{3}O^{+}
Always subtract pOH from 14 for alkalis at 25 °C
steps.narration: Here is a sneaky one. You are given an alkali and you calculate three. That three is the p O H, not the p H! An alkali can never have a p H of three. Always take it away from fourteen. Fourteen minus three gives eleven.

steps.title: Do not assume every salt is neutral
steps.display: Wrong: all salts have pH = 7   |   Right: check hydrolysis and acid salts
working: KHSO_{4}(aq): acidic (acid salt donates H^{+})
steps.narration: Don't assume every salt has a p H of seven. Washing soda in water is alkaline. Ammonium chloride in water is acidic. And an acid salt still has a hydrogen it can give away, so it is acidic too. Ask which parent was weak, and you'll know.

steps.title: One rule to carry into the exam
steps.display: Count real ions: H_{3}O^{+} vs OH^{-}, balanced mole ratios, and salt hydrolysis.
working: pH + pOH = 14   |   \frac{C_{A} V_{A}}{C_{B} V_{B}} = \frac{n_{A}}{n_{B}}   |   Check weak-ion hydrolysis
steps.narration: So what really matters? Count the real ions. Is it hydrogen ions or hydroxide ions? Use the balanced equation for the ratio, never guess one to one. And check whether a salt came from a weak parent. Those three checks will save you many marks.

quickCheck.stem: What is the pH of 0.001 mol/dm^{3} NaOH at 25°C, assuming complete dissociation?

options.why: A pH of 14 corresponds in this model to 1 mol/dm^{3} OH^{-}.
A pH of 13 corresponds to 0.1 mol/dm^{3} OH^{-}.
A pH of 12 corresponds to 0.01 mol/dm^{3} OH^{-}.
The OH^{-} concentration is 10^{-3} mol/dm^{3}, so pOH = 3. At 25°C, pH = 14 − 3 = 11.

steps.title: A hand-to-hand money swap
steps.display: Giver loses cash (oxidised)  →  Receiver gains cash (reduced)
working: No one can gain unless another gives
Oxidation and reduction always happen together
steps.narration: Hand cash to a friend. Your wallet gets lighter. Theirs gets heavier. Electrons move between atoms the same way. One loses, one gains, always together.

steps.title: Rules for assigning oxidation numbers
steps.display: Free element = 0   |   Monatomic ion = charge   |   Sum = 0 (molecule) or ion charge
working: Oxygen = -2 (except peroxides like H_{2}O_{2}: -1; OF_{2}: +2)
Hydrogen = +1 (except metal hydrides like NaH, NaBH_{4}: -1)
Group I metals = +1,  Group II = +2,  Group III = +3
steps.narration: An oxidation number is like a score for each atom. It shows how many electrons it has lost or gained on paper. A free element scores zero. Oxygen usually scores minus two, and hydrogen plus one. Then all the scores must add up to the charge. For a neutral compound, that means zero. Use that to find the one you don't know.

steps.title: Oxidation vs reduction
steps.display: Oxidation: e^{-} loss (O.N. ↑)     |     Reduction: e^{-} gain (O.N. ↓)
working: Zn(s) → Zn^{2+}(aq) + 2e^{-}   (O.N. 0 → +2, oxidation)
Cu^{2+}(aq) + 2e^{-} → Cu(s)   (O.N. +2 → 0, reduction)
Also classically: +O or -H is oxidation; -O or +H is reduction
steps.narration: Here is the easiest way to remember it. OIL RIG. Oxidation is loss of electrons. Reduction is gain. Zinc losing two electrons is oxidised, and its score goes up from zero to plus two. Copper ions gaining two electrons are reduced, and their score goes down to zero. Score up, oxidised. Score down, reduced.

steps.title: Oxidising and reducing agents
steps.display: Oxidising agent accepts e^{-} (is reduced)   |   Reducing agent donates e^{-} (is oxidised)
working: Acidified KMnO_{4} (purple MnO_{4}^{-}) → colourless Mn^{2+} (test for reducing agent)
Acidified K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7} (orange Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}) → green Cr^{3+} (test for reducing agent)
Common reductants: Fe^{2+}, I^{-}, H_{2}S, C, CO, NaBH_{4}
Disproportionation: same species both oxidised and reduced (e.g. KClO_{3})
steps.narration: Now the agents. This part confuses many students, so go slowly. The oxidising agent makes something else lose electrons. To do that, it takes those electrons itself. So the oxidising agent gets reduced. The reducing agent does the opposite, and gets oxidised. Purple permanganate turning colourless tells you a reducing agent is present.

steps.title: Balancing simple redox equations
steps.display: Balance atoms (O with H_{2}O, H with H^{+}), balance charge with e^{-}, equalise e^{-}
working: 1. Split into oxidation and reduction half-equations
2. Balance non-H/O atoms, then O using H_{2}O, then H using H^{+} (acid)
3. Add e^{-} to balance charge on each half
4. Multiply halves so e^{-} lost = e^{-} gained, add and cancel
steps.narration: Balancing redox is like sharing money fairly. Every electron given must be received. So split the reaction into two halves. Balance oxygen with water, then hydrogen with hydrogen ions. Add electrons to fix the charge. Then multiply the halves so the electrons given equal the electrons taken. Add them, and the electrons cancel.

steps.title: Assign oxidation numbers to each half
steps.display: Balance in acid:   Fe^{2+} + MnO_{4}^{-} → Fe^{3+} + Mn^{2+}
working: Oxidation half: Fe^{2+} (+2) → Fe^{3+} (+3)
Reduction half: Mn in MnO_{4}^{-} is +7 (x + 4(-2) = -1) → Mn^{2+} (+2)
steps.narration: Let's try one. Iron goes from plus two to plus three. Its score went up, so iron is oxidised. Now manganese. In permanganate, four oxygens give minus eight, and the ion is minus one. So manganese must be plus seven. It drops to plus two. Score down, so manganese is reduced.

steps.title: Balance O, H, and charge for permanganate
working: Balance O with 4H_{2}O on right; balance H with 8H^{+} on left
Left charge before e^{-}: -1 + 8(+1) = +7; right = +2 → add 5e^{-} on left
steps.narration: Let's fix the manganese half. Four oxygens on the left need four waters on the right. Those waters bring eight hydrogens, so put eight hydrogen ions on the left. Now count charge. The left is plus seven, the right is plus two. Five electrons on the left bring it down to plus two. Balanced.

steps.title: Scale the iron half-equation
working: Each Fe^{2+} loses 1e^{-}; MnO_{4}^{-} gains 5e^{-}
Multiply the iron half by 5 so electrons lost = 5
steps.narration: Manganese takes five electrons. But each iron only gives away one. So we need five irons to supply enough electrons. Multiply the whole iron half by five. Now five electrons are given and five are taken. Fair sharing.

steps.title: Add halves and verify atoms and charge
working: Atoms: 5 Fe, 1 Mn, 4 O, 8 H on both sides
steps.narration: Add the two halves together. The five electrons appear on both sides, so they cancel. Now check. Count every atom on each side, and they match. Check the charge too. Plus seventeen on the left and plus seventeen on the right. When both checks pass, you know you are right.

steps.title: Read the past question
steps.display: In H_{2}O(g) + C(s) → H_{2}(g) + CO(g), which reactant acts as the oxidizing agent?
working: Options: CO(g), C(s), H_{2}O(g), H_{2}(g)
Note: an oxidising agent must be a reactant, not a product
steps.narration: Now a real JAMB question. Steam reacts with hot carbon. Which one is the oxidising agent? Before we start, notice something. Two of the options are products. An agent must be a starting substance. So those two can already be crossed out.

steps.title: Find the oxidation number of every atom
working: Reactants: H = +1, O = -2 in H_{2}O;  C = 0 (free element)
Products: H = 0 in H_{2};  C = +2, O = -2 in CO
steps.narration: Now give every atom its score. In steam, hydrogen is plus one and oxygen is minus two. Carbon on its own is zero. On the other side, hydrogen gas is zero, because it is a free element. In carbon monoxide, oxygen stays minus two, so carbon must be plus two.

steps.title: Identify which species is reduced
steps.display: C: 0 → +2 (oxidised)     |     H in H_{2}O: +1 → 0 (reduced)
working: C increases 0 → +2, so C(s) is oxidised (reducing agent)
H in H_{2}O decreases +1 → 0, so H_{2}O(g) is reduced
steps.narration: Now compare before and after. Carbon went from zero to plus two. Score up, so carbon was oxidised. Hydrogen went from plus one to zero. Score down, so the hydrogen in steam was reduced. Keep that in mind for the final step.

steps.title: Pick the oxidising agent
steps.display: Oxidising agent = H_{2}O(g)  (the reactant that gets reduced)
working: CO(g) and H_{2}(g) are products, not reactants
C(s) is oxidised (reductant); H_{2}O(g) is reduced (oxidant)
steps.narration: Remember the twist. The oxidising agent is the one that gets reduced. Steam was reduced, so steam is the oxidising agent. Carbon was oxidised, so carbon is the reducing agent. And the two products were never in the race.

steps.title: Do not treat hydride H as +1 or flip the sign
working: In metal hydrides (NaH, NaBH_{4}), H is -1 (more electronegative than metal/B)
In NH_{3}: x + 3(+1) = 0 ⇒ N = -3 (do not forget to flip sign from +3)
steps.narration: Hydrogen is usually plus one, but not with metals. In metal hydrides, hydrogen is minus one, because it is the greedier atom there. So in sodium borohydride, boron is plus three. Another slip is signs. In ammonia, three hydrogens give plus three, so nitrogen is minus three, not plus three.

steps.title: Do not pick a product or reverse oxidant vs reductant
steps.display: Wrong: oxidising agent = species oxidised (or a product)   |   Right: reactant that is reduced
working: Fe^{3+} + I^{-} → Fe^{2+} + \frac{1}{2}I_{2}:  I^{-} is oxidised → reducing agent
I_{2} and Fe^{2+} are products, never agents in the forward reaction
steps.narration: The most common redox mistake is mixing up the agents. The one that loses electrons is the reducing agent, not the oxidising agent. Iodide gets oxidised, so iodide is the reducing agent. And never pick a product as an agent. Agents are always on the starting side.

steps.title: Do not confuse dichromate(VI) with permanganate(VII) or ion charge
working: Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-} (heptaoxodichromate(VI)): two Cr atoms share +12 → +6 each
MnO_{4}^{-} (tetraoxomanganate(VII)): x + 4(-2) = -1 → Mn = +7
steps.narration: In dichromate, there are two chromium atoms sharing the charge. Seven oxygens give minus fourteen. The ion is minus two. So the two chromiums together are plus twelve, which is plus six each. Don't report the ion charge as the answer. And don't mix up orange dichromate with purple permanganate.

steps.title: One rule to carry into the exam
steps.display: O.N. ↑ = oxidation (reducing agent)  |  O.N. ↓ = reduction (oxidising agent)
working: Assign every oxidation number first, then balance atoms, electrons, and charge
steps.narration: So here is your exam habit. Give every atom its score first. Score up means oxidised, and that substance is the reducing agent. Score down means reduced, and that substance is the oxidising agent. After that, balance the atoms, the electrons and the charge. Do it in that order every time.

quickCheck.stem: What is the oxidation state of chromium in K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}?

options.why: +7 would make the sum +2 rather than zero.
+5 would make the sum −2.
+4 would make the sum −4.

steps.title: Plating a Spoon with Silver
steps.display: DC power → mobile ions move → new substance forms
working: Battery pushes electrons into the cathode (−)
Dissolved silver ions coat the spoon evenly
steps.narration: Want a silver spoon? Dip it in a silver solution and connect a battery. The electricity pulls silver out of the liquid and coats the spoon.

steps.title: Electrolytes and Electrodes
steps.display: Anode (+): oxidation | Cathode (−): reduction
working: Electrolytes: mobile ions (molten or aqueous)
Non-electrolytes: neutral molecules only (sugar, ethanol)
Cations (+) → Cathode (−) (gain e^{-})
Anions (−) → Anode (+) (lose e^{-})
steps.narration: Electrolysis needs ions that can move. That happens when a salt is melted or dissolved. Sugar water won't work, because sugar makes no ions. Then opposites attract. Positive ions travel to the negative cathode and gain electrons. Negative ions travel to the positive anode and lose electrons. A trick to remember it is PANIC. Positive anode, negative is cathode.

steps.title: Preferential Discharge of Ions
steps.display: Lower ion in series discharges first (unless high halide concentration or active anode)
working: 2. Concentration effect favours halide anions (Cl^{-}, Br^{-}, I^{-})
3. Active anode (Cu, Ag) dissolves instead of discharging anions
4. Mercury cathode discharges Na^{+} preferentially over H^{+}
steps.narration: In water there are many ions, but only one gets discharged at each electrode. Usually it is the one that gives up most easily. Hydrogen ions win over sodium. Hydroxide wins over sulphate. But there are exceptions. Lots of chloride can beat hydroxide. And a copper anode dissolves itself instead.

steps.title: Products at Each Electrode
steps.display: Molten: 2 ions only | Aqueous: compare H^{+}/OH^{-} and electrode
working: Molten PbBr_{2}: Pb at cathode, Br_{2} at anode
Dilute H_{2}SO_{4} (Pt): 2 vol H_{2} (cathode), 1 vol O_{2} (anode)
Brine, conc. NaCl (C): H_{2} (cathode), Cl_{2} (anode), NaOH left
CuSO_{4}(aq): Cu (cathode); O_{2} (Pt anode) or Cu^{2+} (Cu anode)
steps.narration: For a melted salt, it is simple. Only two ions exist, so the metal goes to the cathode and the non-metal to the anode. In water, think harder. Dilute sulphuric acid gives hydrogen and oxygen, two volumes to one. Concentrated brine gives hydrogen and chlorine. Copper sulphate puts copper on the cathode.

steps.title: Faraday's First Law and Q = It
steps.display: Q = It,   n(e^{-}) = \frac{Q}{F},   m = \frac{ItM}{cF}
working: Q in C, I in A, t in s (1 F = 96,500 C/mol e^{-})
M^{c+} + ce^{-} → M needs c moles of e^{-} per mole M
n(M) = \frac{n(e^{-})}{c} = \frac{It}{cF}
STP gas volume = n(gas) × 22.4 dm^{3}/mol
steps.narration: Electricity is just a flow of electrons, and Faraday tells us how to count them. Charge equals current times time, with time in seconds. Divide the charge by ninety six thousand five hundred to get moles of electrons. Then look at the ion charge. A two plus ion needs two electrons for each atom deposited.

steps.title: Faraday's Second Law (Cells in Series)
steps.display: n_{1}c_{1} = n_{2}c_{2}   or   \left(\frac{m}{M}\right)_{1}c_{1} = \left(\frac{m}{M}\right)_{2}c_{2}
working: Same Q in series → same moles of electrons
Moles deposited n ∝ \frac{1}{c} (inverse of ion charge)
1 F deposits 1 mol Ag^{+}, \frac{1}{2} mol Cu^{2+}, \frac{1}{3} mol Al^{3+}
steps.narration: When cells are joined in series, the same current flows through all of them. So they all receive the same number of electrons. But each ion needs a different number. One mole of electrons makes one mole of silver, half a mole of copper, or a third of a mole of aluminium. Bigger charge, fewer atoms.

steps.title: Convert Time and Find Charge Q
steps.display: I = 2.0 A, t = 16 min 5 s → Q = It
steps.narration: Let's try one. The first job is always the time. Amps times seconds gives coulombs, so minutes won't do. Sixteen minutes is nine hundred and sixty seconds. Add five, and we get nine hundred and sixty five seconds. Times two amps gives one thousand nine hundred and thirty coulombs.

steps.title: Convert Charge to Moles of Electrons
steps.narration: Now count the electrons. One mole of electrons carries ninety six thousand five hundred coulombs. So divide our charge by that. One thousand nine hundred and thirty divided by ninety six thousand five hundred gives zero point zero two moles of electrons.

steps.title: Use Half-Equation to Find Mass of Copper
working: 2 mol e^{-} deposit 1 mol Cu
steps.narration: Copper ions are two plus, so each one needs two electrons to become a copper atom. So halve the electrons. Zero point zero two becomes zero point zero one moles of copper. Copper weighs sixty four, so the mass is zero point six four grams.

steps.title: Read the Past Question and Find Charge
steps.display: A current of 5 A flows for 193 s through acidified water. What volume of oxygen forms at STP? Use 96,500 C/mol of electrons and 22.4 dm^{3} per mole of gas.
working: Time is already in seconds: t = 193 s
steps.narration: Now a real JAMB question. This time is already in seconds, which is a gift. So go straight to the charge. Five amps times one hundred and ninety three seconds gives nine hundred and sixty five coulombs.

steps.title: Find Moles of Electrons
working: 1 mol e^{-} carries 96,500 C
steps.narration: Divide by Faraday's number, ninety six thousand five hundred. Look how neatly it works. Nine hundred and sixty five goes into it exactly one hundred times. So we have zero point zero one moles of electrons. JAMB likes numbers that divide nicely like this.

steps.title: Apply the Anode Half-Equation for Oxygen
working: 4 mol e^{-} liberate 1 mol O_{2}
steps.narration: Oxygen comes from hydroxide ions at the anode. Here is the key fact. Four electrons must leave to make just one oxygen molecule. So divide the electrons by four. Zero point zero one over four gives zero point zero zero two five moles of oxygen.

steps.title: Convert Moles of Oxygen to Volume at STP
working: At STP, 1 mol gas occupies 22.4 dm^{3}
steps.narration: Last step, turn moles into volume. Each mole of gas at s.t.p. fills twenty two point four cubic decimetres. Multiply, and you get zero point zero five six. If the options are in cubic centimetres, that is fifty six.

steps.title: Forgetting Ion Charge or Electron Count
steps.display: Wrong: n(metal) = n(e^{-})  |  Right: n = \frac{n(e^{-})}{c}
working: Al^{3+} + 3e^{-} → Al: divide by 3, not 1
steps.narration: The biggest mistake is forgetting how many electrons each particle needs. Aluminium is three plus, so it needs three electrons per atom. Divide by three. Oxygen needs four electrons per molecule, so divide by four. If you skip this step, your answer will be too big.

steps.title: Ignoring Preferential Discharge or Electrode Role
steps.display: Wrong: Na deposits from NaCl(aq)  |  Right: H_{2} forms at cathode
working: In water, H^{+} discharges before Na^{+}; OH^{-} beats SO_{4}^{2-}
Electroplating: object is cathode (−), plating metal is anode (+)
steps.narration: Don't expect sodium metal from salt water. In water, hydrogen ions are easier to discharge, so you get hydrogen gas instead. And for electroplating, remember where things go. The object you want to coat is the cathode. The coating metal is the anode, and it slowly dissolves.

steps.title: Time and Volume Unit Slips
steps.display: Wrong: t in min, or cm^{3} as dm^{3}  |  Right: t in s, 1 dm^{3} = 1,000 cm^{3}
working: 16 min → 16 × 60 = 960 s before Q = It
steps.narration: Two unit slips cost students marks here. First, time must be in seconds. Sixteen minutes is not sixteen. It is nine hundred and sixty seconds. Second, watch your volumes. One cubic decimetre is a thousand cubic centimetres. So fifty six cubic centimetres is zero point zero five six cubic decimetres.

steps.title: One Sentence to Remember
steps.display: Pick the winning ions at each electrode, then link charge Q = It through moles of electrons and ion charge c.
working: Cathode = reduction, Anode = oxidation, n(product) = \frac{It}{cF}
steps.narration: So here is the full picture. First decide which ion wins at each electrode. Then count the electrons. Current times time gives charge. Charge over Faraday gives moles of electrons. Divide by the ion charge, and you have your product.

quickCheck.stem: A quantity of electricity liberates 3.6 g of silver from its salt. What mass of aluminium would the same quantity of electricity liberate from its salt? Take Al = 27 and Ag = 108.

options.why: 2.7 g is nine times the mass from the shared electron amount.
1.2 g comes from dividing the silver mass by three while ignoring the different molar masses.
0.9 g accounts for molar mass but ignores the three electrons needed per aluminium ion.

\frac{3.6}{108} mol of silver uses the same number of moles of electrons because Ag^{+} needs one each. Each Al^{3+} needs three, so aluminium mass is \left(\frac{3.6}{108}\right) × \frac{27}{3} = 0.30 g.

lessons.title: Atomic structure and the periodic table

steps.title: A Marble on a Football Pitch
steps.display: Tiny heavy nucleus (p^{+} + n^{0})  |  Wide electron shells (e^{-})
working: Centre marble = protons + neutrons (almost all mass)
Stands around pitch = fast electrons driving chemistry
steps.narration: Picture a marble on the centre spot of a football pitch. That marble is the nucleus. It holds almost all the weight. Tiny electrons race around the stands.

steps.title: Protons, Neutrons, Electrons, Z and A
working: Proton (+1, mass 1) and Neutron (0, mass 1) in nucleus
Electron (-1, mass \frac{1}{1840}) in shells outside nucleus
Neutral atom: e^{-} = p^{+}; Cation M^{q+}: e^{-} = Z - q
Anion X^{q-}: e^{-} = Z + q
steps.narration: Every atom has three kinds of particles. Protons are positive and sit in the middle. Neutrons have no charge and sit there too. Electrons are negative and move around outside. The atomic number counts protons only. The mass number counts protons plus neutrons. So to find neutrons, take the small number from the big one.

steps.title: Isotopes and Relative Atomic Mass
working: Isotopes: same Z (protons, chemistry), different A (neutrons, mass)
steps.narration: Isotopes are twins. Same number of protons, so they behave the same in reactions. But different neutrons, so they weigh differently. That is why chlorine is thirty five point five, not a whole number. Most chlorine atoms weigh thirty five, and some weigh thirty seven. The average leans toward the common one.

steps.title: Shells and s, p, d Electron Configuration
working: Max per shell = 2n^{2}: K(2), L(8), M(18), N(32)
Subshell capacity: s(2), p(6), d(10), f(14); 2 e^{-} per orbital (Pauli)
Hund: fill degenerate orbitals singly before pairing
Exceptions: Cr = [Ar] 3d^{5}4s^{1}, Cu = [Ar] 3d^{10}4s^{1}
steps.narration: Electrons live in shells, and shells have rooms called s, p and d. Fill the lowest rooms first. Think of bus seats filling from the front. An s room holds two, a p holds six, and a d holds ten. In a p room, electrons sit alone before they pair up. Strangers always take empty seats first.

steps.title: How Configuration Sets Group, Period and Block
steps.display: Period = highest n  |  Main Group = valence e^{-} (ns + np)
working: Modern table orders by increasing atomic number Z
Mg (3s^{2}): n = 3 (Period 3), 2 valence e^{-} (Group II / 2, s-block)
Cl (3s^{2} 3p^{5}): 7 valence e^{-} (Group VII / 17, halogen, p-block)
He (1s^{2}), Ne, Ar: full outer shell (Group 0 / 18, noble gases)
steps.narration: Your electron arrangement tells you where an element lives on the table. The highest shell number gives the period. Count all the electrons in that outer shell, both s and p, and that gives the group. So chlorine, with seven outside, is in Group seven. A full outer shell means a noble gas.

steps.title: Periodic Trends Across Periods and Down Groups
steps.display: Across Period (→): radius ↓, IE ↑, EA ↑, EN ↑
working: Down Group (↓): more shells, shielding ↑, radius ↑, IE ↓, EN ↓
Metallic character: decreases across period (→), increases down group (↓)
Group I reactivity ↑ down group (easier valence e^{-} loss)
Group VII reactivity ↓ down group (harder e^{-} gain)
steps.narration: Here is how to reason about trends. Going across a period, protons increase, so the nucleus pulls harder. Atoms get smaller and hold their electrons more tightly. Going down a group, you add whole new shells. Atoms get bigger and lose outer electrons more easily. That is why the alkali metals get more reactive as you go down.

steps.title: Count Protons, Neutrons and Electrons in ^{31}_{15}P
working: Protons = Z = 15
Electrons (neutral atom) = 15
Neutrons = A - Z = 31 - 15 = 16
steps.narration: Let's try one with phosphorus. The small number, fifteen, gives the protons. A neutral atom has the same number of electrons, so fifteen electrons too. For neutrons, take fifteen from thirty one. That gives sixteen.

steps.title: Write the s, p, d Configuration and Check Hund's Rule
working: Remaining 3 electrons: 3p_{x}^{1} 3p_{y}^{1} 3p_{z}^{1}
3 unpaired electrons (Hund's rule)
steps.narration: Now place fifteen electrons into rooms, lowest first. One s, two s, two p and three s take twelve of them. That leaves three for the three p rooms. They spread out, one in each, before pairing. So phosphorus has three unpaired electrons.

steps.title: Deduce Period, Block and Group
steps.display: 3s^{2} 3p^{3}  →  Period 3, p-block, Group V (15)
working: Highest occupied shell n = 3 → Period 3
Valence electrons = 2 + 3 = 5 → Group V (IUPAC 15)
Outer electron enters 3p → p-block non-metal
steps.narration: Now find its home on the table. The highest shell is three, so phosphorus is in period three. Count the outer electrons. Two in s plus three in p makes five. So it is in Group five. Its last electron went into a p room, so it is a p block element.

steps.title: Read the Isotope Ratio Question
steps.display: Element X has two isotopes with mass numbers 20 and 22, present in the ratio 1:3. What is the relative atomic mass of X?
working: Mass numbers: A_{1} = 20,  A_{2} = 22
Ratio parts: R_{1} = 1,  R_{2} = 3
steps.narration: Now a real JAMB question. There are two kinds of atoms, weighing twenty and twenty two. For every one light atom, there are three heavy ones. So imagine a small bag of just four atoms. One weighs twenty, and three weigh twenty two.

steps.title: Sum the Weighted Contributions
working: Lighter isotope contribution: 20 × 1 = 20
Heavier isotope contribution: 22 × 3 = 66
Total ratio parts: 1 + 3 = 4
steps.narration: Weigh the whole bag. The light atom gives twenty. The three heavy atoms give sixty six. Together, the bag weighs eighty six. And there are four atoms in the bag.

steps.title: Divide by Total Parts to Get A_{r}
working: Closer to 22 than 20 because ratio favours 22
steps.narration: For the average, share the weight across the four atoms. Eighty six over four is twenty one point five. Does it make sense? Yes. Most of the atoms are the heavy kind, so the average should sit closer to twenty two than to twenty.

steps.title: Counting Only p Electrons as Valence Electrons
steps.display: Wrong: 3s^{2} 3p^{5} has 5 valence e^{-}  |  Right: 2 + 5 = 7 valence e^{-}
working: Valence shell = ALL electrons in highest n (both ns and np)
1s^{2} 2s^{2} 2p^{6} 3s^{2} 3p^{5}: 7 outer electrons → Group VII (17)
steps.narration: A common trap is looking only at the last group of electrons. Three p five does not mean five outer electrons. The outer shell is the whole third shell, so you must add the two s electrons too. Two plus five gives seven. That puts it in Group seven, with the halogens.

steps.title: Mixing Up Nucleons, Mass Number and Electrons
steps.display: Wrong: n^{0} = A, or e^{-} in nucleus  |  Right: n^{0} = A - Z
working: Nucleus contains ONLY protons and neutrons (nucleons)
Tritium ^{3}_{1}H: 1 proton, 3 - 1 = 2 neutrons (no e^{-} inside)
steps.narration: Don't mix up mass number and neutrons. The mass number counts protons and neutrons together. So neutrons are the mass number minus the protons. And electrons never live in the nucleus. Tritium has mass three and one proton, so it has two neutrons.

steps.title: Unweighted Isotope Averages and Period Radius Traps
steps.display: Wrong: \frac{20+22}{2} = 21.0; radius ↑ across period
working: Right: weight each isotope by its abundance or ratio
Right: across a period (→), higher nuclear charge shrinks atomic radius
steps.narration: Two more traps. Never just add isotope masses and halve them. Twenty and twenty two do not give twenty one, unless they are equally common. Weight them by how common they are. And atoms get smaller across a period, not bigger, because the stronger nucleus pulls the electrons in.

steps.title: One Sentence to Remember
steps.display: Protons fix identity and isotopes give weighted mass, while outer s and p electrons govern group, period and periodic trends.
working: Z = p^{+}, A_{r} = weighted mean, Period = max n, Group = valence e^{-}
steps.narration: So remember this. Protons decide which element it is. Isotopes are weighted by how common they are. And the outer electrons decide the period, the group and how the element behaves. Learn to count those three things, and most atom questions are easy.

quickCheck.stem: Which statement is true of an atom with configuration 1s^{2} 2s^{2} 2p^{6} 3s^{2} 3p^{5}?

options.text: Its outer p subshell is full
options.why: The outer 3p subshell can hold six electrons and has only five.

options.text: It has five electrons in its outer shell
options.why: The outer shell contains two 3s electrons as well as five 3p electrons.
Group 2 atoms normally have two valence electrons.
The valence configuration 3s^{2} 3p^{5} has seven electrons, characteristic of Group 17. This atom is chlorine, a halogen.

steps.title: Handing Over, Sharing, or Pooling Together
steps.display: Transfer (ionic)  |  Equal share (covalent)  |  One gives both (dative)  |  Shared sea (metallic)
working: Ionic: one hands over, one receives
Covalent: both contribute equally to share
Dative: one friend pays for both
steps.narration: Friends can share in different ways. One can hand over money completely. Two can each put in. One can pay for both. Atoms bond in these same ways.

steps.title: Ionic (Electrovalent) Bonding
steps.display: Metal (low IE) + Non-metal (high EA)  →  M^{m+} + X^{x-}  →  M_{x}X_{m}
working: Large electronegativity difference favours electron transfer
Non-directional electrostatic attraction builds a giant crystal lattice
steps.narration: Ionic bonding is a handover. A metal has a few outer electrons it wants to get rid of. A non-metal wants a few more. So the metal gives them away and becomes positive. The non-metal takes them and becomes negative. Opposite charges pull together. Sodium gives one electron to chlorine, and you get salt.

steps.title: Covalent and Dative (Coordinate) Bonding
steps.display: Covalent: A· + ·B → A:B   |   Dative: A: + B → A→B
working: Single (H-H), double (O=O), triple (N≡N) shared electron pairs
Non-polar (H_{2}, Cl_{2}: equal EN) vs polar (H-Cl, H_{2}O: unequal EN)
Dative: donor lone pair + acceptor empty orbital (NH_{3} + H^{+} → NH_{4}^{+})
Once formed, a dative bond behaves identically to a covalent bond
steps.narration: Covalent bonding is sharing. Two non-metals each put one electron in, and they share the pair. Two pairs make a double bond, three make a triple. In a dative bond, one atom brings both electrons. Ammonia gives its spare pair to a hydrogen ion. Once formed, you can't tell it apart from an ordinary covalent bond.

steps.title: Metallic Bonding
steps.display: Positive metal ions  ↔  mobile sea of delocalised valence e^{-}
working: Metals have low ionisation energies and vacant valence orbitals
Mobile electrons carry electric current and thermal energy
Non-directional bonding allows ion layers to slip without shattering
Explains lustre, malleability, ductility and high melting points
steps.narration: In a metal, the atoms let their outer electrons go free. Those electrons flow around like a sea, and the metal ions sit inside it. That moving sea explains a lot. It carries electricity and heat. It also lets layers slide without breaking, so you can hammer a metal into a pot.

steps.title: Van der Waals Forces and Hydrogen Bonds
steps.display: Dispersion (weakest) < Dipole-dipole < Hydrogen bond (F, O, N) << Covalent
working: Van der Waals dispersion: acts between all molecules (holds I_{2}, Ar, CH_{4})
Dipole-dipole: aligns permanent dipoles in polar molecules (HCl)
Hydrogen bond: H bonded to F, O or N attracts lone pair on nearby F, O or N
H-bonding raises b.p. of H_{2}O, HF, NH_{3}, alkanols; makes ice open and less dense
steps.narration: These are the weak pulls between whole molecules, not inside them. The weakest is van der Waals, and every molecule has some. Stronger is the hydrogen bond. It only happens when hydrogen is stuck to fluorine, oxygen or nitrogen. That is why water boils at a hundred degrees, while similar small molecules are gases.

steps.title: Shapes of Simple Molecules (VSEPR)
steps.display: Electron pairs repel → maximum separation around central atom
working: 2 BP, 0 LP → linear, 180° (CO_{2}, BeCl_{2}, C_{2}H_{2}); 3 BP, 0 LP → trigonal planar, 120° (BF_{3})
4 BP, 0 LP → tetrahedral, 109.5° (CH_{4}, NH_{4}^{+})
3 BP, 1 LP → trigonal pyramidal, 107° (NH_{3}); 2 BP, 2 LP → bent or V-shape, 105° (H_{2}O)
Symmetrical shapes (CO_{2}, CH_{4}, CCl_{4}) cancel bond dipoles → non-polar molecule
steps.narration: Electron pairs push each other away, so they spread out as far as they can. Two pairs make a straight line. Four pairs make a three dimensional pyramid shape, like methane. But spare pairs push harder. In water, two spare pairs squeeze the bonds, so water is bent, not straight.

steps.title: Properties That Follow from Bonding
steps.display: Structure + Bond Type  →  Melting point, Solubility, Conductivity, Hardness
working: Ionic crystals: high m.p., brittle, soluble in water, conduct when molten or aqueous
Simple molecular: low m.p./b.p., soft, non-conductors (unless ionised in water)
Giant covalent: diamond (3D, non-conductor) vs graphite (2D layers, conducts)
Polar water dissolves ions (ion-dipole) and H-bonding molecules (like dissolves like)
steps.narration: Once you know the bond, you can predict how a substance behaves. Ionic solids melt at high temperatures and conduct only when melted or dissolved. Small molecules melt easily and don't conduct. Diamond is very hard. Graphite conducts, because it has free electrons between its layers. Like dissolves like.

steps.title: Classify Potassium Chloride and Water
steps.display: Compare KCl (_{19}K + _{17}Cl) and H_{2}O (_{1}H + _{8}O)
working: _{19}K (2,8,8,1): Group I metal;  _{17}Cl (2,8,7): Group VII non-metal
_{1}H (1) and _{8}O (2,6): both non-metals
steps.narration: Let's try one. Always start by asking, metal or non-metal? Potassium has one outer electron, so it is a Group one metal. Chlorine has seven, so it is a non-metal. Hydrogen and oxygen are both non-metals.

steps.title: Assign Bond Types and Shape
steps.display: KCl: K^{+}Cl^{-} (ionic)   |   H_{2}O: bent (105°), polar + H-bonds
working: K loses 1 e^{-} → K^{+}; Cl gains 1 e^{-} → Cl^{-} (electrostatic lattice)
O shares 2 pairs with H (2 BP, 2 LP) → V-shape (105°), polar molecule
O-H groups form intermolecular hydrogen bonds between H_{2}O molecules
steps.narration: A metal with a non-metal means a handover. Potassium gives one electron to chlorine, so potassium chloride is ionic. Two non-metals means sharing. Oxygen shares with two hydrogens and keeps two spare pairs. Those spare pairs bend the molecule. And water can hydrogen bond, because hydrogen is stuck to oxygen.

steps.title: Predict Melting, Solubility and Conductivity
steps.display: KCl: high-m.p. solid, conducts molten/aq   |   H_{2}O: liquid, dissolves KCl
working: KCl solid: ions locked in lattice → non-conductor; molten/aq: mobile ions → conducts
H_{2}O: liquid at room temp (H-bonds); polar molecules hydrate K^{+} and Cl^{-}
steps.narration: Now predict the behaviour. Potassium chloride is a hard solid that melts at a high temperature. It only conducts when melted or dissolved, because then its ions can move. Water is a liquid, held together by hydrogen bonds. Its bent, polar molecules pull the ions apart, so the salt dissolves.

steps.title: Read the Ammonium Chloride Bonding Question
steps.display: Which bond types are needed in the textbook account of crystalline NH_{4}Cl, including how NH_{4}^{+} forms from NH_{3} and H^{+}?
working: Choices: (a) Ionic and covalent   (b) Ionic and coordinate
(c) Ionic, covalent and coordinate   (d) Covalent, coordinate and metallic
steps.narration: Now a real JAMB question, from twenty fifteen. Ammonium chloride is a salt, but it has no metal. That is the clue. We need to look at three places. Inside ammonia, how ammonia picks up a hydrogen ion, and how the ions pack together.

steps.title: Check the Bonds Inside Ammonia (NH_{3})
steps.display: N (2,5) + 3 H (1)  →  3 ordinary covalent N-H bonds + 1 lone pair
working: Each H contributes 1 e^{-}; N contributes 1 e^{-} per bond (3 shared pairs)
Rule out any choice missing ordinary covalent bonds
steps.narration: Start inside ammonia. Nitrogen shares one electron with each of three hydrogens. That makes three normal covalent bonds. Nitrogen still has one spare pair left over. Remember that pair. So any option without covalent bonds is already wrong.

steps.title: Trace Formation of Ammonium Ion (NH_{4}^{+})
steps.display: H_{3}N: + H^{+}  →  [NH_{4}]^{+}   (dative / coordinate covalent bond)
working: H^{+} has an empty 1s orbital and brings zero electrons
N donates both electrons of its lone pair → coordinate bond
Rule out any choice missing coordinate bonding
steps.narration: Now the hydrogen ion comes along. It has no electrons at all, just an empty space. So nitrogen gives its spare pair to share. Both electrons come from nitrogen. That is a dative bond. So any option missing dative bonding is wrong too.

steps.title: Check Crystal Packing and Rule Out Metallic Bonding
steps.display: NH_{4}^{+} + Cl^{-}  →  NH_{4}^{+}Cl^{-} (ionic lattice, no metal)
working: Oppositely charged NH_{4}^{+} and Cl^{-} ions attract electrostatically (ionic)
No metal atoms or delocalised electron sea → eliminate metallic
steps.narration: Finally, the positive ammonium ion and the negative chloride ion attract each other. That is ionic bonding. Is there metallic bonding? No, there is no metal at all. So the answer needs ionic, covalent and dative. All three.

steps.title: Boiling Overcomes Intermolecular Forces, Not Covalent Bonds
steps.display: Wrong: boiling H_{2}O or I_{2} breaks covalent bonds (or H-bonds in I_{2})
working: Right: boiling H_{2}O/alkanols breaks intermolecular H-bonds; O-H bonds stay intact
Right: I_{2} has no H atom → molecular lattice held by van der Waals forces
Right: ice floats because H-bonds hold H_{2}O molecules in an open lattice
steps.narration: Boiling water does not break water molecules apart. The bonds inside each molecule stay whole. Boiling only breaks the weak pulls between molecules. And don't say iodine has hydrogen bonds. It has no hydrogen! Its molecules are held together by van der Waals forces.

steps.title: Why Ionic Crystals Shatter While Metals Bend
steps.display: Wrong: shifting salt layers bends it; solid NaCl conducts current
working: Right: shifting ionic layers aligns like charges (+ near +) → repulsion → fracture
Right: ionic compounds conduct only when molten or aqueous (mobile ions)
Right: metal layers slip inside non-directional electron sea → malleable
steps.narration: Why does salt shatter while metal bends? Push a salt crystal, and like charges slide next to each other. They repel, and the crystal cracks. Push a metal, and the electron sea keeps holding it together, so it just bends. Also, solid salt does not conduct. Its ions are locked in place.

steps.title: Flat Paper Drawings Hide 3D Shapes and Dipole Cancellation
steps.display: Wrong: CH_{4} is flat 90°; CO_{2} is polar because C=O is polar
working: Right: CH_{4} has 4 equal C-H bond pairs → 3D tetrahedral (109.5°)
Right: CO_{2} is linear (180°) → equal opposite C=O dipoles cancel (non-polar)
steps.narration: Paper drawings can fool you. Methane looks flat when drawn, but it is really three dimensional, with angles of one hundred and nine point five. And carbon dioxide has polar bonds, but it is a straight line. The two pulls are equal and opposite, so they cancel. The molecule is non-polar.

steps.title: One Sentence to Remember
steps.display: Electron transfer, sharing or pooling builds the bond; 3D electron repulsion sets shape; lattice or intermolecular forces explain properties.
working: Intramolecular (ionic, covalent, dative, metallic) vs intermolecular (van der Waals, H-bond)
steps.narration: So remember three ideas. How electrons are handed over, shared or pooled decides the bond. Electron pairs pushing apart decide the shape. And the pulls between particles decide melting, dissolving and conducting. Ask about all three, and bonding questions get much easier.

quickCheck.stem: The molecular lattice of iodine is held together by

options.why: A coordinate bond involves a donated electron pair. The question asks what holds distinct molecules together.
Metallic bonding requires delocalised electrons in a metal lattice.
I_{2} contains no hydrogen and does not form hydrogen bonds.
Iodine forms discrete I_{2} molecules. Its molecular crystal is held together by London dispersion forces, a type of van der Waals attraction.

steps.title: Giving a Molecule a Clear Street Address
steps.display: Longest carbon road (root) + closest landmark (number) + family surname (suffix)
working: Main road = longest continuous carbon chain
House number = position closest to the functional group
Surname = family suffix (-ane, -ene, -yne, -ol, -oic acid, -oate)
steps.narration: Naming a carbon molecule is like writing an address. Find the longest road. Number from the end nearest the landmark. End with the family surname.

steps.title: Homologous Series and Carbon Root Names
steps.display: Consecutive homologues differ by -CH_{2}- (mass 14)   |   Root = longest chain
working: Shared general formula & functional group → similar chemical reactions
Physical properties (b.p., density) rise steadily as chain length grows
Roots: C1 meth-, C2 eth-, C3 prop-, C4 but-, C5 pent-, C6 hex-
C7 hept-, C8 oct-, C9 non-, C10 dec-; branches use -yl (CH_{3}- = methyl)
steps.narration: Organic compounds come in families called homologous series. Each member is one C H two bigger than the one before. They react the same way, but they boil at higher temperatures as they get bigger. The first part of the name counts the carbons. Meth is one, eth is two, prop is three, but is four.

steps.title: Functional Groups Set the Family and Suffix
steps.display: -ane (C-C)  |  -ene (C=C)  |  -yne (C≡C)  |  -ol (-OH)  |  -oic acid (-COOH)  |  -oate (-COO-)
working: Alkanes (C_{n}H_{2n+2}): single bonds only (saturated); suffix -ane
Alkenes (C_{n}H_{2n}): C=C double bond (unsaturated); suffix -ene
Alkynes (C_{n}H_{2n-2}): C≡C triple bond (unsaturated); suffix -yne
Alkanols (-OH, -ol), alkanoic acids (-COOH, -oic acid), esters (-COO-, -oate)
steps.narration: The ending of the name tells you the family. Only single bonds? It ends in ane. A double bond? Ene. A triple bond? Yne. An O H group makes it an alcohol, ending in ol. A C O O H group makes an acid, ending in oic acid. And esters end in oate.

steps.title: Naming Alkanes, Alkenes and Alkynes
steps.display: Longest chain (with C=C or C≡C) → lowest locant → alphabetical prefixes
working: Alkanes: number from end nearest first branch (CH_{3}CH(CH_{3})CH_{2}CH_{3} = 2-methylbutane)
Alkenes/alkynes: number from end nearest multiple bond (but-1-ene, but-2-yne)
Use di-, tri-, tetra- for repeated groups; commas between numbers, hyphens before letters
Alphabetise distinct substituents ignoring di-/tri- (bromo before chloro before methyl)
steps.narration: To name a chain, first find the longest one. If there is a double or triple bond, it must be inside that chain. Then number from the end that gives the bond or branch the smallest number. Two methyl groups become dimethyl. And list different branches in alphabetical order.

steps.title: Naming Alkanols and Alkanoic Acids
steps.display: Alkanol: alkane - e + -ol (propan-1-ol)   |   Acid: alkane - e + -oic acid
working: Alkanols (R-OH): number chain to give -OH carbon the lowest number
Primary (RCH_{2}OH), secondary (R_{2}CHOH), tertiary (R_{3}COH, e.g. 2-methylpropan-2-ol)
Alkanoic acids (R-COOH): -COOH carbon is ALWAYS C1 (included in chain count)
HCOOH = methanoic (formic) acid; CH_{3}COOH = ethanoic (acetic) acid
steps.narration: For alcohols, number the chain so the O H gets the smallest number. Propan one ol has it at the end. For acids, there is good news. The acid carbon is always number one, and you count it in the chain. So methanoic acid has one carbon, and ethanoic acid has two.

steps.title: Naming Esters (Alkanoates, RCOOR')
steps.display: RCOOH (acid) + R'OH (alkanol)  ⇌  RCOOR' (alkyl alkanoate) + H_{2}O
working: Two-word name: alkyl group R' (from alcohol) + acid root with -oate
R' attaches to the single-bonded oxygen (-O-R'); acid chain includes C=O carbon
HCOOCH_{3} → methyl (from CH_{3}OH) + methanoate (from HCOOH)
CH_{3}COOC_{2}H_{5} → ethyl ethanoate (familiar name: ethyl acetate)
steps.narration: An ester is made when an acid joins an alcohol. Its name has two words. The first word comes from the alcohol. The second word comes from the acid, ending in oate. So the methyl part sits on the single bonded oxygen. And the acid part includes the carbon with the double bonded oxygen.

steps.title: Structural and Geometric Isomerism
steps.display: Same molecular formula, different connectivity (structural) or spatial layout (cis/trans)
working: Chain isomers: butane vs 2-methylpropane (both C_{4}H_{10})
Position isomers: propan-1-ol vs propan-2-ol (both C_{3}H_{8}O)
Functional group isomers: ethanol (CH_{3}CH_{2}OH) vs methoxymethane (CH_{3}OCH_{3})
Geometric (cis-trans): restricted C=C rotation + two different groups on EACH C=C carbon
steps.narration: Isomers have the same formula but a different arrangement, like the same Lego bricks built differently. Butane can be a straight chain or a branched one. Both have four carbons and ten hydrogens. Geometric isomers are different. They need a double bond, which can't twist. Each carbon of that bond also needs two different groups.

steps.title: Find Chain and Functional Group in CH_{3}CH(OH)CH_{2}CH_{3}
steps.display: Name CH_{3}CH(OH)CH_{2}CH_{3}   and   CH_{3}CH_{2}COOCH_{3}
working: First compound: 4 carbons in continuous chain → root but-
Functional group is -OH → alkanol, suffix -ol
steps.narration: Let's try the first one. Count the carbons in the longest chain. There are four, so the name starts with but. Now find the family. There is an O H group, so it is an alcohol. The ending will be ol.

steps.title: Number Closest to -OH
steps.display: CH_{3}-CH(OH)-CH_{2}-CH_{3}  →  1-2-3-4 gives -OH at C2 → butan-2-ol
working: Left to right puts -OH on carbon 2; right to left puts -OH on carbon 3
Lowest locant is 2 → butan-2-ol (a secondary alkanol)
steps.narration: Now where is the O H? Count from the left, and it sits on carbon two. Count from the right, and it sits on carbon three. Always choose the smaller number. So the name is butan two ol.

steps.title: Split the Ester CH_{3}CH_{2}COOCH_{3}
steps.display: CH_{3}CH_{2}COO-  (3-carbon acid part)   |   -CH_{3} (1-carbon alcohol part)
working: Alkyl group on single-bonded oxygen: -CH_{3} → methyl
Acid part including carbonyl carbon: CH_{3}CH_{2}COO- (3 carbons) → propanoate
steps.narration: Now the ester. Find the single bonded oxygen, and cut there. On one side, there is a C H three group. One carbon, so that is methyl. On the other side is the acid part. Count its carbons, and include the one with the double bonded oxygen. Three carbons, so propanoate.

steps.title: Assemble the Two-Word Ester Name
steps.display: CH_{3}CH_{2}COOCH_{3}  →  methyl propanoate
working: Alkyl part first (methyl) + acid -oate part second (propanoate)
Answers: butan-2-ol and methyl propanoate
steps.narration: Put the two words together, alcohol part first. Methyl, then propanoate. So the answers are butan two ol and methyl propanoate. Notice that we named the ester by splitting it, not by counting all four carbons together.

steps.title: Read the Ester and Alkyne Naming Question
steps.display: What are the names of HCOOCH_{3} and HC≡CH, in that order?
working: Choices: (a) Methyl methanoate and ethene   (b) Methanoic acid and ethyne
(c) Ethyl methanoate and ethyne   (d) Methyl methanoate and ethyne
steps.narration: Now a real JAMB question, from twenty fifteen. We need to name two compounds, in the right order. The first is H C O O C H three. The second is two carbons joined by a triple bond. Let's take them one at a time.

steps.title: Identify HCOOCH_{3} as an Ester, Not an Acid
steps.display: HCOOCH_{3} has -COO- bonded to -CH_{3} (ester), not -COOH (acid)
working: Methanoic acid would be HCOOH (ends in H, not CH_{3})
Eliminate the choice calling HCOOCH_{3} methanoic acid
steps.narration: Look at the end of the first formula. It ends in C H three, not just H. An acid ends in O H. So this is not methanoic acid. It is an ester. Any option calling it an acid is out.

steps.title: Name the Alcohol and Acid Halves of HCOOCH_{3}
steps.display: HCOO- (1 C: methanoate) + -CH_{3} (1 C: methyl)  →  methyl methanoate
working: Alcohol alkyl group is -CH_{3} (methyl), NOT -C_{2}H_{5} (ethyl)
Acid part HCOO- has 1 carbon → methanoate
Eliminate the choice giving ethyl methanoate
steps.narration: Now split the ester at the single bonded oxygen. The alcohol side has one carbon, so it is methyl, not ethyl. The acid side, H C O O, has one carbon, so it is methanoate. That gives methyl methanoate.

steps.title: Name HC≡CH and Confirm the Order
steps.display: HC≡CH (2 C, triple bond)  →  ethyne (acetylene), not ethene (C=C)
working: 2 carbons → eth-; triple bond (≡) → -yne → ethyne
Ethene has a double bond (CH_{2}=CH_{2}); eliminate the choice with ethene
Correct order: methyl methanoate and ethyne
steps.narration: The second compound has two carbons, so it starts with eth. A triple bond means the ending is yne. So it is ethyne. Ethene would need a double bond, so that option is out. Our answer is methyl methanoate and ethyne, in that order.

steps.title: Reversing the Two Halves of an Ester
steps.display: Wrong: CH_{3}CH_{2}COOCH_{3} is ethyl propanoate  |  Right: methyl propanoate
working: Alcohol alkyl group (-O-R') comes FIRST; carbonyl chain (R-COO-) gives -oate
HCOOCH_{3}: -CH_{3} (methyl) + HCOO- (methanoate), NOT ethyl or acid
steps.narration: The most common ester mistake is swapping the two halves. Always find the single bonded oxygen. Whatever sits on it gives the first word. The side with the double bonded oxygen gives the second word. So this ester is methyl propanoate, not ethyl propanoate.

steps.title: Counting Bent Chains or Different Formulas as Isomers
steps.display: Wrong: C_{4}H_{10} has 3 or 4 isomers; C_{2}H_{6}O and C_{3}H_{6}O are isomers
working: Right: isomers MUST have the exact same molecular formula
Right: bending an unbranched chain does NOT make a new isomer
C_{4}H_{10} has only 2 isomers: butane and 2-methylpropane
steps.narration: Two isomer traps. First, isomers must have exactly the same formula. If the formulas differ, they are not isomers. Second, bending a straight chain on paper does not make a new compound. Butane has only two isomers, the straight chain and the branched one.

steps.title: Expecting Cis-Trans Isomerism on Terminal Alkenes
steps.display: Wrong: prop-1-ene (CH_{3}CH=CH_{2}) has cis-trans isomers
working: Right: EACH C=C carbon must carry two different groups (a ≠ b and e ≠ f)
Terminal =CH_{2} has two identical H atoms → NO cis-trans isomerism
Internal alkenes like hex-3-ene or but-2-ene DO show geometric isomerism
steps.narration: A double bond is not enough for geometric isomers. Each carbon in the double bond needs two different groups. Prop one ene ends with a carbon holding two hydrogens. They are the same, so there are no geometric isomers. But hex three ene has different groups on both sides, so it works.

steps.title: One Sentence to Remember
steps.display: Longest chain gives the root, functional group gives the suffix, lowest numbering places branches and multiple bonds, and same formula with different layout gives isomers.
working: Root (chain) + lowest locants + suffix (family)  |  Check formula first for isomers
steps.narration: So naming has three steps. The longest chain gives the start of the name. The family gives the ending. And the smallest numbers show where things sit. For isomers, always check the formula first. Practise a few, and naming becomes automatic.

options.why: Each carbon of the double bond in hex-3-ene carries a hydrogen and an ethyl group. Restricted rotation therefore allows distinct geometric isomers.
Hexane has no double bond to restrict rotation.
Prop-1-ene has two hydrogens on the terminal alkene carbon.
3-Methylbut-1-ene also has two hydrogens on its terminal alkene carbon.

steps.title: Diced yam and balanced crowds
steps.display:
Smaller pieces cook faster (reaction rate)
Equal people entering and leaving a hall (equilibrium)
steps.narration: Diced yam boils faster than a whole tuber because more surface meets hot water. Equilibrium is like a busy market where people enter and leave at equal speeds.

steps.title: Reaction rate and collision theory
steps.display:
Rate = \frac{Δ(concentration or volume)}{Δt}
Effective collision: E ≥ E_{a} AND proper orientation
working: Steepest upward slope on a volume–time curve = fastest rate
Horizontal flat part of the curve = reaction has stopped (rate = 0)
Activation energy (E_{a}) = minimum energy barrier for reaction
steps.narration: Particles must bump into each other to react. But not every bump works. They need enough energy, called the activation energy, and they must hit the right way. On a volume against time graph, the steepest part is the fastest. When the line goes flat, the reaction has finished.

steps.title: Factors affecting reaction rate
steps.display: Higher T, concentration, gas pressure, or surface area → faster rate
working: Concentration or gas pressure ↑ → more particles per volume → more collisions
Powder > chips > lump → larger solid surface area → shorter reaction time
Temperature ↑ → faster motion and more particles with E ≥ E_{a}
Nature of reactants: aqueous ionic reactions are faster than covalent ones; light aids photolysis
