steps.narration: Anything that makes useful collisions happen more often speeds a reaction up. More concentration means more particles crowded together. Smaller pieces mean more surface to hit. That is why powder reacts faster than a lump. Heat makes particles move faster, and more of them have enough energy. It is the same reason diced yam cooks faster.

steps.title: Catalysts and enzymes
steps.display: Catalyst lowers E_{a} via an alternative path (regenerated unchanged)
working: Lowers forward and reverse E_{a} equally → equilibrium reached faster
Does NOT change ΔH, total product yield, or equilibrium composition
Enzymes are biological catalysts (e.g. zymase; dehydrogenase in redox)
steps.narration: A catalyst is a shortcut. It gives the reaction an easier path with a lower energy hill. So more particles make it over, and the reaction speeds up. But the catalyst is not used up. It speeds both directions equally, so you get the same amount of product. You just get it sooner. Enzymes are catalysts in living things.

steps.title: Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium
steps.display: aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD  |  Rate_{forward} = Rate_{reverse} ≠ 0
working: Requires a closed system so gases or vapour cannot escape
Concentrations remain constant (not necessarily equal)
K_{c} = \frac{[C]^{c}[D]^{d}}{[A]^{a}[B]^{b}}  (exclude pure solids and liquids)
steps.narration: Some reactions go both ways at once. At equilibrium, the forward and backward speeds are equal. Nothing looks like it is changing, but both reactions are still running. Think of a hall where people enter and leave at the same rate. The crowd stays the same size. This only works in a closed container.

steps.title: Le Chatelier's principle (concentration, pressure, temperature)
steps.display: Stress applied → equilibrium shifts to oppose the stress
working: Concentration: add reactant or remove product → shifts right; add common ion → shifts away
Pressure ↑ (gases): shifts toward FEWER gas moles (if equal gas moles, no shift)
Temperature ↑: favours endothermic direction (ΔH > 0); ONLY temperature changes K_{c}
Inert gas added at constant volume: no shift in equilibrium position
steps.narration: Le Chatelier's principle is simple. If you disturb an equilibrium, it moves to undo what you did. Add a reactant, and it uses some up by moving right. Squeeze gases, and it moves to the side with fewer gas molecules. Heat it, and it moves the way that absorbs heat. Only temperature changes the value of K c.

steps.title: Write the equilibrium constant K_{c}
working: Given at equilibrium: [SO_{2}] = 0.2, [O_{2}] = 0.5, [SO_{3}] = 0.4 mol dm^{−3}
Put products on top and reactants below, each raised to its coefficient
steps.narration: Let's try one. To write K c, products go on top and reactants go below. Each concentration is raised to the power of its number in the equation. So sulphur trioxide is squared on top. Sulphur dioxide is squared below, times oxygen.

steps.title: Substitute equilibrium concentrations
steps.narration: Now put in the numbers. On top, zero point four squared is zero point one six. Below, zero point two squared is zero point zero four. Times zero point five gives zero point zero two. Squaring small decimals is where many students slip, so take your time here.

steps.title: Compute K_{c} and check units
steps.narration: Zero point one six divided by zero point zero two gives eight. What about the units? There are two concentrations on top and three below. So one is left below. That gives per mole, cubic decimetres.

steps.title: Predict pressure shift at constant T
steps.display:
Reactants: 2 + 1 = 3 mol gas  |  Product: 2 mol gas
Higher P → shifts right; K_{c} stays 8
working: Compression favours the side with fewer gas moles (2 < 3)
Constant temperature keeps K_{c} unchanged at 8 mol^{−1} dm^{3}
steps.narration: Now what if we raise the pressure? Count the gas molecules. The left has two plus one, so three. The right has two. Pressure pushes towards fewer gas molecules, so the equilibrium moves right. But temperature did not change, so K c is still eight.

steps.title: Read the JAMB question
steps.display:
For the exothermic equilibrium P(g) + Q(g) ⇌ 3R(s) + S(g),
which change increases the yield of R?
working: States matter: P, Q, S are gases (g), while R is a solid (s)
Gas moles: 2 mol on left (P + Q) vs 1 mol on right (S only)
steps.narration: Now a real JAMB question. Here is the key detail. R is a solid. P, Q and S are gases. When we think about pressure, solids don't count. So the left has two gas molecules, and the right has only one.

steps.title: Test using a larger closed vessel
steps.display: Larger vessel → lower pressure → favours more gas moles
working: Left has 2 mol gas; right has 1 mol gas (ignore solid R)
Equilibrium shifts left → yield of R decreases
steps.narration: Try a bigger vessel first. More space means lower pressure. Lower pressure favours the side with more gas molecules. That is the left side. Moving left makes less R. So this option is wrong.

steps.title: Test increasing the temperature
steps.display: Forward is exothermic (ΔH < 0) → reverse is endothermic
working: Heating favours the endothermic reverse direction
Equilibrium shifts left → yield of R decreases
steps.narration: Try heating. The forward reaction gives out heat. So the backward reaction must take heat in. Heating favours the side that absorbs heat, which is backward. That makes less R. Wrong again.

steps.title: Test catalyst and removing S
steps.display:
Positive catalyst: no change in equilibrium yield
Removing S(g): equilibrium shifts right → more R(s)
working: A positive catalyst speeds forward and reverse rates equally
Removing gaseous S pulls equilibrium right to replace S, forming more R
steps.narration: A catalyst speeds both directions equally, so the amount of R does not change. Now try removing S. The equilibrium wants to replace what you took away. So it moves right to make more S. And moving right also makes more R. That is our answer.

steps.title: Catalysts never increase total yield or shift equilibrium
steps.display:
Wrong: Catalyst makes more total product or shifts equilibrium right
Right: Catalyst only lowers E_{a}, reaching the same yield sooner
working: Equal H_{2}O_{2} samples give equal total O_{2} with or without MnO_{2}
Forward and reverse activation energies drop equally, so K_{c} is unchanged
steps.narration: A catalyst never gives you more product. It only gets you there faster. If you decompose two equal samples of hydrogen peroxide, one with a catalyst, both give the same oxygen in the end. The catalyst one just finishes first. So a catalyst never shifts the equilibrium.

steps.title: Count only gases for pressure, and watch equal gas moles
steps.display:
Wrong: Pressure always shifts equilibrium, or solids count as gas volume
Right: Count only (g) moles; equal gas moles (Δn = 0) → no shift
working: A(g) ⇌ B(g) or H_{2}(g) + I_{2}(g) ⇌ 2HI(g): equal gas moles → no shift
2CO(g) + O_{2}(g) ⇌ 2CO_{2}(g): 3 mol gas → 2 mol gas → compression shifts right
steps.narration: Pressure only matters for gases. Count the gas molecules on each side, and ignore solids and liquids. And if both sides have the same number, pressure does nothing. Hydrogen plus iodine making two hydrogen iodide has two on each side. So squeezing it causes no shift.

steps.title: Equilibrium is dynamic, and temperature changes K_{c}
steps.display:
Wrong: Reactions stop at equilibrium, or K_{c} never changes
Right: Forward and reverse rates stay equal; heating changes K_{c}
working: Exothermic forward (ΔH < 0): heating shifts left → K_{c} decreases
Endothermic forward (ΔH > 0): heating shifts right → K_{c} increases
steps.narration: At equilibrium, the reaction has not stopped. Both directions keep going at the same speed. And the amounts on each side don't have to be equal. Also, K c is not fixed forever. Temperature changes it. Heat an exothermic reaction, and K c gets smaller.

steps.title: Collisions set speed; opposition sets shift
steps.display:
Rate ↑ with effective collisions per second
Equilibrium opposes stress; only temperature alters K_{c}
steps.narration: So keep two ideas separate. Speed is about collisions. More useful collisions per second means a faster reaction. Equilibrium is about balance. Disturb it, and it moves to undo the change. And only temperature changes the value of K c.

quickCheck.stem: Which combination gives the highest rate of carbon dioxide production?

options.text: 0.05 mol dm^{−3} HCl and 5 g powdered CaCO_{3}
options.why: This uses powder but a weaker acid concentration.

options.text: 0.05 mol dm^{−3} HCl and a 5 g lump of CaCO_{3}
options.why: This uses both a lower concentration and a lump with less exposed surface.

options.text: 0.10 mol dm^{−3} HCl and 5 g powdered CaCO_{3}
options.why: Powder exposes more calcium carbonate surface, and the 0.10 mol dm^{−3} acid has the highest concentration. Together these give the highest collision rate and fastest carbon dioxide production.

options.text: 0.025 mol dm^{−3} HCl and 5 g powdered CaCO_{3}
options.why: This uses powder with the lowest acid concentration listed.

steps.title: Cooking firewood and instant cold packs
steps.display:
Burning firewood → heat flows out (warms the pot)
Cold pack salt dissolving → heat flows in (chills your hand)
steps.narration: Burning firewood pushes heat out into your cooking pot and kitchen air. Dissolving an instant cold pack pulls heat from your hand, making the pack feel chilly.

steps.title: Exothermic, endothermic and sign of ΔH
steps.display:
ΔH = ΣH_{products} − ΣH_{reactants}
Exothermic: ΔH < 0  |  Endothermic: ΔH > 0
working: Exothermic: heat released to surroundings → temperature rises (ΔH is −)
Endothermic: heat absorbed from surroundings → temperature falls (ΔH is +)
Carbon(IV) oxide (carbon dioxide): C(s) + O_{2}(g) → CO_{2}(g), ΔH° = −393 kJ mol^{−1}
steps.narration: Every reaction either gives out heat or takes it in. If it gives out heat, the surroundings get warmer. That is exothermic, and delta H is negative. If it takes heat in, the surroundings get colder. That is endothermic, and delta H is positive. Burning carbon gives out heat, so its delta H is negative.

steps.title: Energy profile diagrams
steps.display:
Exothermic: E_{products} < E_{reactants} (step down)
Endothermic: E_{products} > E_{reactants} (step up)
working: Top of the curve = transition state (activated complex)
Activation energy: E_{a} = E_{peak} − E_{reactants} (always positive)
Enthalpy arrow: from reactant level to product level (ΔH = E_{products} − E_{reactants})
steps.narration: An energy profile is like walking over a hill. You start at the reactants' height. You must climb to the top first, and that climb is the activation energy. Then you come down to the products. If you end lower than you started, energy was given out. If you end higher, energy was taken in.

steps.title: Heats of reaction, combustion and neutralisation
steps.display: q = m c ΔT  |  ΔH = ± \frac{q}{n}
working: Combustion (ΔH_{c}°): 1 mol burns completely in excess O_{2} (always −)
Neutralisation (ΔH_{n}°): 1 mol H_{2}O formed; strong acid + strong base = −57.3 kJ mol^{−1}
Weak acid or base gives |ΔH_{n}°| < 57.3 kJ mol^{−1} (ionisation absorbs heat)
Water c = 4.2 or 4.18 J g^{−1} K^{−1} (use the value given in the question)
steps.narration: To measure heat, use the water. Mass times specific heat times temperature change gives the heat. Then divide by the moles. Heat of combustion is for burning one mole, so it is always negative. Heat of neutralisation is for making one mole of water. A weak acid gives less heat, because some energy goes into breaking it apart.

steps.title: Heat of solution and Hess's law
steps.display: ΔH_{soln} = ΔH_{lattice dissociation} + ΔH_{hyd}
working: Breaking the crystal lattice absorbs energy (+); hydrating ions releases energy (−)
Hydration energy > lattice separation energy → exothermic (ΔH_{soln} < 0)
Hess's law: total ΔH depends only on initial and final states, not the route
steps.narration: Dissolving a salt happens in two parts. First the crystal must be pulled apart, which takes energy in. Then water surrounds the ions, which gives energy out. Compare the two. If more comes out than goes in, dissolving is exothermic. And Hess's law says the route doesn't matter. Only the start and the end count.

steps.title: Bond energies and spontaneity
steps.display: ΔH = ΣE(bonds broken) − ΣE(bonds formed)
working: Breaking reactant bonds absorbs energy (endothermic, +)
Forming product bonds releases energy (exothermic, −)
Spontaneity check: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (ΔG < 0 spontaneous; T in K = °C + 273)
steps.narration: Breaking a bond always takes energy in. Making a bond always gives energy out. So delta H is the energy you put in to break bonds, minus the energy you get back from making new ones. Whether a reaction happens on its own depends on delta G. If delta G is negative, it is spontaneous.

steps.title: Count bonds broken and formed
working: Bonds broken in reactants: 1 H−H bond and 1 Cl−Cl bond
Bonds formed in products: 2 H−Cl bonds
steps.narration: Let's try one. Before any numbers, count the bonds. On the left, we break one hydrogen to hydrogen bond and one chlorine to chlorine bond. On the right, we make two hydrogen to chlorine bonds. Two, because there are two molecules of hydrogen chloride.

steps.title: Sum energy absorbed breaking bonds
steps.display: ΣE(bonds broken) = 436 + 242 = 678 kJ
working: Bond breaking is endothermic (+)
steps.narration: Breaking bonds costs energy. So add up what we spend. Four hundred and thirty six for the hydrogen bond, plus two hundred and forty two for the chlorine bond. That comes to six hundred and seventy eight kilojoules taken in.

steps.title: Sum energy released forming bonds
steps.display: ΣE(bonds formed) = 2 × 431 = 862 kJ
working: Two moles of H−Cl form, so multiply 431 by 2
steps.narration: Making bonds pays energy back. Each hydrogen to chlorine bond gives four hundred and thirty one. We make two of them. So we get eight hundred and sixty two kilojoules back.

steps.title: Subtract formed from broken
working: 862 kJ released > 678 kJ absorbed → net exothermic
steps.narration: Now subtract what we got back from what we spent. Six hundred and seventy eight minus eight hundred and sixty two gives minus one hundred and eighty four. It is negative because we got back more than we spent. So the reaction gives out heat. It is exothermic.

steps.title: Read the JAMB question
steps.display:
At 25°C, a system has a free energy change of −899 J mol^{−1} and an entropy change of 10 J mol^{−1} K^{−1}.
Calculate the enthalpy change.
working: Given: t = 25 °C, ΔG = −899 J mol^{−1}, ΔS = 10 J mol^{−1} K^{−1}
Required: ΔH in J mol^{−1}
steps.narration: Now a real JAMB question. We are given delta G, which is minus eight hundred and ninety nine. We are given delta S, which is ten. The temperature is twenty five degrees. We need to find delta H.

steps.title: Convert Celsius to Kelvin
working: JAMB convention uses T(K) = t(°C) + 273
Both ΔG and ΔS are already in joules, so no kJ conversion is needed
steps.narration: First, the temperature. Never use Celsius in this formula! Add two hundred and seventy three to get two hundred and ninety eight kelvin. Then check the units. Both values are already in joules, so nothing needs converting. That is one less trap.

steps.title: Rearrange the free energy equation
steps.display: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS  ⇒  ΔH = ΔG + TΔS
steps.narration: The formula is delta G equals delta H minus T delta S. We want delta H, so move T delta S to the other side. Delta H equals delta G plus T delta S. Now work out T delta S. Two hundred and ninety eight times ten gives two thousand nine hundred and eighty.

steps.title: Substitute and find ΔH
working: +2980 exceeds −899, giving a positive (endothermic) ΔH
steps.narration: Now add. Minus eight hundred and ninety nine plus two thousand nine hundred and eighty gives two thousand and eighty one. It is positive. So this reaction takes heat in. It is endothermic, and that matches one of the options.

steps.title: Never reverse bond-energy or profile signs
steps.display:
Wrong: ΔH = ΣE(formed) − ΣE(broken), or exothermic products higher
Right: ΔH = ΣE(broken) − ΣE(formed); exothermic products sit lower
working: Breaking a bond always absorbs energy (+)
Forming a bond always releases energy (−)
steps.narration: Don't flip the formula. It is bonds broken minus bonds formed, never the other way round. Breaking always takes energy in. Making always gives energy out. And on an energy diagram, an exothermic reaction ends lower than it started, not higher.

steps.title: Convert °C to Kelvin and match energy units
steps.display:
Wrong: T = 25 in TΔS, or mixing kJ with J
Right: T = 25 + 273 = 298 K; keep ΔH and TΔS in matching units
working: Using 25 instead of 298 K gives −649 J mol^{−1} (a classic trap)
If ΔH is in kJ and ΔS is in J K^{−1}, divide ΔS by 1000
steps.narration: This is the classic trap in this topic. If you use twenty five instead of two hundred and ninety eight, you get minus six hundred and forty nine. That will be one of the options, waiting for you! Always change to kelvin. And if one value is in kilojoules and another in joules, make them match first.

steps.title: Cold surroundings mean endothermic, not exothermic
steps.display:
Wrong: Solution turns cold → heat left system (ΔH < 0)
Right: Solution turns cold → system absorbed heat (ΔH > 0); check ΔG for spontaneity
working: Cold pack cools water and hand because dissolving absorbs heat (ΔH > 0)
Exothermic ΔH < 0 alone does not guarantee spontaneity; ΔG = ΔH − TΔS decides
steps.narration: If a beaker feels cold, heat did not leave the reaction. The reaction pulled heat out of the water and your hand. So it absorbed heat, and delta H is positive. That is how a cold pack works. Also, a negative delta H alone does not prove a reaction is spontaneous. Check delta G.

steps.title: Follow the heat flow
steps.narration: So follow the heat. If heat flows out and things get warmer, delta H is negative. If heat flows in and things get colder, delta H is positive. For bond energies, always take broken minus formed. Keep those three ideas, and energy questions become steady marks.

quickCheck.stem: What describes dissolution of an ionic solid when the energy released by hydration exceeds the energy required to separate the lattice?

options.why: Spontaneity also depends on the entropy change.
An endothermic process has a positive enthalpy change.
The solution enthalpy is the positive lattice separation energy plus the negative hydration enthalpy. The net enthalpy change is negative.
Reversibility cannot be determined from the two energy magnitudes alone.
